claims.evidence: This is an observation from the optogenetic experiments, shown in Figure 5D, with citations to similar findings in adult brain.

claims.claim: The biphasic response pattern of INs to inhibition is typical for inhibition-stabilized networks (ISNs).
claims.source: This response pattern is typical for inhibition-stabilized networks (ISNs), a regime at which adult cortical circuits operate (Sanzeni et al., 2020; Sadeh et al., 2017), and that has been suggested to not characterize the early developing brain (Rahmati et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Optogenetic IN stimulation results in decreased STTC values.
claims.source: IN stimulation resulted in decreased STTC values (main IN stimulation effect, p<10–71, 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model) (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the optogenetic experiments with statistical support, shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Optogenetic IN inhibition increases STTC.
claims.source: On the other hand, IN inhibition increased STTC (main IN inhibition effect, p<10–286, 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model) (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the optogenetic experiments with statistical support, shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: IN modulation has a larger impact on STTC values of nearby neurons when compared to pairs that are further apart.
claims.source: Moreover, in line with the strongest decorrelation along development for nearby neurons (Figure 3D), IN modulation had a larger impact on STTC values of nearby neurons when compared to pairs that are further apart (IN stimulation*distance interaction, p=2*10–4; IN inhibition*distance interaction p<10–5, 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model) (Figure 6C–D).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the optogenetic experiments with statistical support, shown in Figures 6C-D.

claims.claim: GE mice have reduced excitatory activity in the superficial layers of the mPFC.
claims.source: GE mice mimic the etiology (combined disruption of Disc1 gene and maternal immune activation) and cognitive impairment of schizophrenia, showing already at neonatal age reduced excitatory activity in the superficial layers of the mPFC (Chini et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2019; Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is based on previously published data, with citations.

claims.claim: Deep layers of the mPFC are not affected in GE mice.
claims.source: On the flipside, deep layers of the mPFC are not affected.
claims.evidence: This is stated based on previously published data.

claims.claim: GE mice have lower STTC values than controls.
claims.source: Overall, GE mice had lower spike train correlations when compared to controls (main condition effect, p=0.032, 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of the GE mouse data with statistical support.

claims.claim: The STTC deficit in GE mice depends on whether the neuron pair is situated in the superficial or deep layers of the mPFC.
claims.source: In line with the proposed hypothesis, this deficit depended on whether the neuron pair was situated in the superficial or deep layers of the mPFC (condition*layer interaction, p<10–7, 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of the GE mouse data with statistical support.

claims.claim: There is no significant difference between STTC of controls and GE spike train pairs situated in the deep layers.
claims.source: While there was no significant difference between STTC of controls and GE spike train pairs situated in the deep layers (p=0.15, 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model), spike train pairs of GE mice in which one of the two neurons was located in the superficial layers had reduced STTC values (p=0.016, 1 s lag).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of the GE mouse data with statistical support.

claims.claim: Spike train pairs of GE mice in which one of the two neurons is located in the superficial layers have reduced STTC values.
claims.source: While there was no significant difference between STTC of controls and GE spike train pairs situated in the deep layers (p=0.15, 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model), spike train pairs of GE mice in which one of the two neurons was located in the superficial layers had reduced STTC values (p=0.016, 1 s lag).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of the GE mouse data with statistical support.

claims.claim: The STTC difference is more robust if both neurons are situated in the superficial layers in GE mice.
claims.source: This difference was even more robust if both neurons were situated in the superficial layers (p=10–3, 1 s lag) (Figure 7B–D).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of the GE mouse data with statistical support, shown in Figures 7B-D.

claims.claim: The 1/f exponent increases with age in newborn babies between 36 and 45 post-conception weeks.
claims.source: We quantified the 1/f exponent on the 1–20 Hz frequency range and confirmed that it increased with age (age coefficient = 0.26, 95% CI [0.24; 0.27], p<10–183, linear model) (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of human EEG data with statistical support, shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: The 1/f exponent increases with age in babies recorded at 40 and 43 PCW.
claims.source: The analyses revealed that also for these data the PSD slope grew steeper (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B-C) and the 1/f exponent increased with age (age coefficient = 0.30, 95% CI [0.17; 0.42], p<10–4, linear mixed-effect model) (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of human EEG data with statistical support, shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: The increase in 1/f slope over age is similar across two different human EEG datasets.
claims.source: The increase in 1/f slope over age was very similar across the two different datasets (mean age coefficients = 0.26 and 0.30) and no statistical difference was found between them (main dataset effect, p=0.15; age*dataset interaction, p=0.21, linear mixed-effect model) (Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of human EEG data with statistical support, shown in Figure 8E.

claims.claim: The E-I ratio decreases along development in newborn humans.
claims.source: Thus, the E-I ratio decreases along development also in newborn humans.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the human EEG data analysis.

claims.claim: The developmental decrease in E-I ratio might represent a fingerprint of cortical circuit maturation in mammalian species.
claims.source: This feature might represent a fingerprint of cortical circuit maturation in mammalian species.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings in both mice and humans.

results.result: During early postnatal development (P2-P12) in the mouse mPFC, multiple measures of neural activity increase with age, including the proportion of active periods, maximum amplitude of active periods, broadband LFP power, and single unit firing rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 provide converging quantitative evidence with statistical support (all p<10^-9) showing monotonic or exponential increases in multiple activity measures across development. These findings are internally consistent and well-documented with appropriate statistical modeling.

results.result: The 1/f exponent of the power spectral density increases with age in the developing mouse mPFC (P2-P12), indicating a developmental shift in E-I ratio toward inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 establish the theoretical link between 1/f exponent and E-I ratio through citations to prior work. Claims C52-C53 provide direct experimental evidence with strong statistical support (p<10^-27) that the 1/f exponent increases with age, supporting the inference of decreased E-I ratio during development.

results.result: Neural network modeling demonstrates that increased net inhibition strength leads to both an increase in the 1/f exponent and a logarithmic decrease in spike train correlations (STTC).
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 present computational modeling results with quantitative parameters and statistical support. The model uses biologically plausible parameters and demonstrates the mechanistic link between inhibition strength, 1/f exponent, and neural correlations, providing theoretical support for the experimental findings.

results.result: Spike train correlations (STTC) in the developing mouse mPFC decrease with age and distance between neurons, with nearby neuron pairs showing more severe decorrelation over development than distant pairs.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60 provide comprehensive experimental evidence with strong statistical support (p<10^-78 for distance, p<10^-4 for age, p<10^-12 for interaction) from analysis of >40,000 spike train pairs. The spatial specificity of the decorrelation effect strengthens the finding and is consistent across multiple timescales.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of interneurons results in widespread inhibition of putative pyramidal neurons, with the proportion of inhibited neurons increasing with age, supporting that GABA exerts inhibitory effects from early postnatal days.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 provide direct experimental evidence from optogenetic manipulations with statistical support (p=0.005 for age effect). The rebound excitation after stimulus termination and consistency with adult brain patterns strengthen the conclusion. However, the inference about GABA's inhibitory role (C64) relies on population-level effects and modeling support rather than direct single-cell measurements.

results.result: In the mouse mPFC, GABA has an inhibitory role already at P2 and the cortex operates in an inhibition-stabilized network (ISN) regime from the first postnatal days.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 are supported by converging evidence from optogenetic experiments showing population-level inhibition and neural network modeling demonstrating that only hyperpolarizing GABA (Vrev ≥10 mV below Vrest) can recapitulate observed dynamics. The biphasic response of INs to inhibition is characteristic of ISN networks, though this conclusion challenges prior hypotheses about developmental timing.

results.result: Optogenetic inhibition of interneurons causes widespread increases in pyramidal neuron firing that augment with age, while interneurons display a biphasic response characteristic of inhibition-stabilized networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 provide experimental evidence with strong statistical support (p<10^-8 for age effect) and are consistent with prior work in adult brain (C70-C71 cite relevant studies). The biphasic IN response provides additional evidence for ISN operation, though the authors note this contradicts some prior developmental hypotheses.

results.result: Optogenetic manipulation of interneuron activity causally modulates spike train correlations: IN stimulation decreases STTC while IN inhibition increases STTC, with stronger effects on nearby neuron pairs.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 provide direct causal evidence with extremely strong statistical support (p<10^-71 for stimulation, p<10^-286 for inhibition) linking IN activity to neural correlations. The spatial specificity (distance interaction effects) strengthens the mechanistic interpretation and connects to the developmental decorrelation findings.

results.result: GE mice, a model of neurodevelopmental disorders with reduced excitatory activity in superficial mPFC layers, show layer-specific reductions in spike train correlations, with the strongest deficits when both neurons are in superficial layers.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C81 analyze an existing dataset and demonstrate layer-specific STTC deficits with statistical support (p=0.032 overall, p=10^-3 for both superficial). The spatial specificity matching the known anatomical deficits (C75-C76) strengthens the interpretation that altered E-I ratio causes correlation deficits. However, C75-C76 rely on previously published data rather than new measurements.

results.result: The 1/f exponent increases with age in human newborns (36-45 post-conception weeks), indicating that E-I ratio decreases during early human brain development, potentially representing a conserved feature of mammalian cortical maturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 provide strong quantitative evidence from two independent human EEG datasets with very strong statistical support (p<10^-183 and p<10^-4) and consistent effect sizes (0.26 and 0.30). Claims C85-C86 draw inferences about E-I ratio and evolutionary conservation based on the established link between 1/f exponent and E-I ratio, though direct measurement of E-I ratio in humans is not possible with EEG.

results.result: A relative increase of inhibition mechanistically drives the decorrelation of neural activity, and changes in E-I ratio control neural activity (de)correlation.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C8 represent the central mechanistic conclusion of the study, supported by converging evidence from neural network modeling (C54-C55), developmental observations (C52-C53, C56-C60), and causal optogenetic manipulations (C72-C74). The integration of computational, observational, and interventional approaches provides strong support for this mechanistic link.

results.result: In the mouse mPFC during the first two postnatal weeks, neural activity decorrelates following specific spatial patterns, accompanied by a shift in E-I ratio toward inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 summarize key experimental findings that are well-supported by the detailed results in C44-C60. The spatial specificity of decorrelation (nearby neurons more affected) and the concurrent E-I ratio shift (inferred from 1/f exponent) are both documented with strong statistical evidence.

results.result: In mice modeling neurodevelopmental disorders, subtle alterations in E-I ratio are associated with specific impairments in spike train correlations, suggesting that developmental E-I imbalance might contribute to neurodevelopmental disorder pathogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claim C6 is directly supported by the GE mouse data (C77-C81) showing layer-specific correlation deficits. Claim C9 is more speculative but reasonably supported by the mechanistic link established in the study and the anatomical specificity of the deficits. The use of 'might contribute' appropriately reflects the correlational nature of this evidence.

results.result: An analogous developmental transition in E-I ratio takes place in the human brain.
results.evaluation: Claim C7 is supported by the human EEG data (C82-C84) showing increased 1/f exponent with age. While the inference about E-I ratio relies on the established relationship from prior work (C48-C51), the consistency across two independent datasets and the parallel with mouse findings strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Throughout development, the brain transitions from highly synchronous to sparse and decorrelated activity, which allows for more efficient information processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 represent established knowledge in the field (evidence_type: KNOWLEDGE) that provides context for the study. While not directly tested here, these claims are well-supported by the cited literature and the current study's findings are consistent with this framework.

results.result: Neural activity in the developing brain across multiple species has unique characteristics including discontinuity, low firing rates, loose E-I coordination, and weak behavioral state modulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C18 summarize prior work (all evidence_type: CITATION) establishing the characteristics of developing brain activity across species. These provide important context but are not novel findings of this study. The citations appear appropriate for establishing this background.

results.result: As brain networks mature, multiple features change including increased rhythmicity and complexity of oscillations, decreased E-I ratio, tighter temporal E-I coordination, and decorrelation/sparsification of activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C23 summarize established developmental processes from prior literature (all evidence_type: CITATION). These provide essential context for the current study's focus on the mechanistic relationship between E-I ratio and decorrelation, but are not novel findings.

results.result: The relationship between decorrelation and E-I ratio has been extensively studied in adult brains, and decorrelated/sparse activity is functionally important for efficient information processing in both biological and artificial neural networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 establish prior work on E-I ratio and decorrelation in adult systems (all evidence_type: CITATION). These provide important motivation for studying this relationship during development but represent background knowledge rather than novel findings.

results.result: Prior to this study, it was unknown whether changes in E-I ratio underlie developmental decorrelation, direct evidence linking E-I ratio to developmental decorrelation was lacking, and the inhibitory role of GABA in early development was debated.
results.evaluation: Claims C28, C40-C41 identify knowledge gaps that motivate the study (evidence_type: KNOWLEDGE). These accurately characterize the state of the field and justify the research questions, though they are not findings themselves.

results.result: Altered E-I ratio is hypothesized to be a hallmark of neurodevelopmental disorders including autism and schizophrenia, which have been linked to disrupted correlated activity in animal models.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 summarize prior hypotheses and findings about E-I ratio in neurodevelopmental disorders (all evidence_type: CITATION). These provide important clinical context and motivation but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: During cortical development, pyramidal neurons and interneurons migrate following an inside-out sequence, with interneurons showing protracted integration dominated initially by SST+ cells and later by PV+ cells, with inhibitory synapse development continuing until P30.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C37 summarize established developmental neurobiology (evidence_type: CITATION or KNOWLEDGE) that provides context for understanding the E-I ratio changes. These are well-established facts that motivate the study but are not novel findings.

results.result: The developmental strengthening of inhibitory synapses and tilting of E-I ratio toward inhibition might underlie neural activity decorrelation, supported by evidence that chronic IN manipulation alters brain activity structure.
results.evaluation: Claim C38 presents a hypothesis based on prior work (C21, C37), while C39 provides supporting evidence from prior studies (evidence_type: CITATION). These establish the rationale for the current study's experiments but are not novel findings themselves.

results.result: There has been a long-standing hypothesis that GABA acts as an excitatory neurotransmitter in early rodent neocortex, but this hypothesis has been challenged by recent work.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C43 describe a scientific controversy in the field (evidence_type: CITATION) that the current study addresses. These provide important context for interpreting the optogenetic results but are not findings of this study.
